name: Stayza
tagline: Verified, commission-free student housing in Pakistan
summary: A trusted accommodation marketplace for students: verified hostels, shared flats and private rooms with direct owner contact and zero commission. I founded it and run product, engineering, hiring and QA.

stages.note: Deployed on a custom domain with integrated email services.

overview: Stayza is a full stack web platform designed to simplify hostel discovery for students. As the founder and developer, I built the application from the ground up, including authentication, hostel listings, verification workflows, dashboards, deployment, and ongoing product improvements.
problem: Students searching for accommodation often rely on scattered information from social media, messaging groups, and personal recommendations. Stayza centralizes hostel information into a single platform, making it easier to discover, compare, and connect with hostel owners.
implementation: Developed the frontend with React and TypeScript, integrated Supabase for authentication and backend services, designed the PostgreSQL database, implemented role based access control, and deployed the application to production using Vercel.

name: CampusFlow
tagline: A time-aware schedule assistant for university students
summary: An offline-first Android app that turns a static timetable into one live answer: what is happening now, and where to go next. Countdowns, room-aware transitions, schedule exceptions, LLM-assisted import and a home-screen widget. Ships as CampusFlow by Stayza.

stages.note: PRD v2.2 and TRD v1.1 written before code.

overview: CampusFlow answers one question a timetable never does: "What am I supposed to do right now, and where do I go next?" The core interaction is Open, Glance, Know, Go.
problem: Timetables are static grids. A student at 10:56 AM does not need the whole week; they need the next class, the room, and how long until they should leave. Calendar apps get part of the way there but cannot represent free periods, room-to-room transitions or one-off exceptions without clutter.
implementation: Built with Expo and React Native in TypeScript. Schedules live in local SQLite so the app works fully offline, with optional Supabase sync. A schedule engine derives NOW/NEXT states and countdowns from the clock instead of storing them, and a native Android widget shows the next class on the home screen.
Getting a timetable in is the usual churn point, so CampusFlow ships an LLM-assisted import: run the provided prompt against a photo of your timetable in any chat app and paste the JSON back.

name: Madad
tagline: An offline semantic search engine for course material
summary: Point Madad at a semester of PDFs, slides, Word files and scans and it answers queries in milliseconds, entirely offline. A Python Brain ingests, embeds and classifies; a C++ Engine searches with data structures written from scratch.

overview: Madad (مدد, "help") is a local-first study search engine. It is deliberately not a chatbot: the contribution is the search and retrieval system. An optional Ask Mode over a local LLM is a thin demonstration layer on top.
problem: Students collect hundreds of course files a semester across LMS downloads, chat groups and folders. Before an exam, finding the one slide that explains a concept, or every past question on a topic, takes hours.
architecture: Two independently testable halves joined by a frozen, versioned file contract (CRC32-checked). The Python Brain handles ingestion, parsing, OCR, chunking, TF-IDF and embeddings, topic classifiers and evaluation. It never searches.

The C++ Engine never embeds or trains. It builds every index from scratch: an FNV-1a hash table with chaining, an inverted index with BM25, KD-tree, LSH and HNSW for vectors, a trie for autocomplete, an AVL tree, a binary heap for top-K, and a concept graph with BFS, DFS and Dijkstra learning paths.
implementation: Hybrid search fuses BM25 and semantic results. Budgets: keyword search under 50 ms and semantic under 100 ms at 10,000 chunks, autocomplete under 10 ms. Built as the joint semester project for CS250 (Data Structures) and CS272 (Artificial Intelligence).

name: Smart Academic File Organizer
tagline: Watches your downloads and files every course document for you
summary: A desktop assistant that watches the Downloads folder, extracts text from PDFs, slides, Word files, images and archives, scores each file against your enrolled courses with a six-signal confidence engine, and moves it into Semester / Course / Type folders. Every move is undoable, and every file is full-text searchable.

overview: A lightweight Python utility that automatically organizes academic files into a structured directory hierarchy.
implementation: Automated file discovery, folder creation, and document organization using Python to simplify academic file management.
